  {"slot": 3, "score": 0.70, "why": "Strong protections: no surgery-gated LGR, X markers, hate-crime statute, marriage, courts restoring care access; but record 227 aggregated hate crimes, agency abolished, no national GI anti-discrimination law, prison-housing decree, deteriorating climate."},

Dossier 1: Singapore-like. Same-sex decriminalized 2022. No LGR without surgery (resident). No anti-discrimination including GI. Media regulator restricts "homosexual lifestyle" — but that's LGB-focused broadcast code; the gender-neutral toilet backlash is social friction/hostility (tier 3 mild). Prison: 10 trans inmates, no recorded assaults. Pride rally 28,000. Youth survey: 80% willing to work with LGBTQ. Travel operator describes thriving LGBTQ scene. No documented police targeting of trans people. No trans-specific violence documented. Border practice unknown. No criminalisation of trans identity. So: no trans-specific criminal offence, no documented targeting, but social acceptance is ambivalent (gender-neutral toilet backlash, broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia). Overall this is a relatively safe destination — Reduced Risk band, maybe 0.62-0.68. Hmm. Let me think.

Rule 13: no trans-specific criminal offence, no documented targeting, no documented social acceptance of gender diversity (no third-gender tradition). So sits a step below acceptance-with-protections tier. The backlash over gender-neutral toilets is social hostility toward trans inclusion — moderate. But actual risk to traveler if outed: social disapproval, possible service friction, media code irrelevant. No criminal exposure. Facilities: gender-neutral toilets rare; bathroom use in practice not legally restricted. Trans visitor in gendered spaces — no law banning. So the main risk is social disapproval/tier 3-ish with thin recourse (no anti-discrimination for GI; but hate crime? not documented). Also Section 294 public decency — could in principle apply but no trans enforcement documented.

I'd put around 0.60-0.65. Let's say 0.62.

Dossier 2: Article 489 criminalises same-sex "indecent acts," used to arrest trans people on basis of gender expression. Documented police abuse (forced genital display), forced outing via posting ID documents, no LGR, no anti-discrimination, authorities block LGBT orgs, 21% say homosexuality acceptable, official hostility ("trash"). Documented pattern of targeting by police. That's tier 2 (state-tolerated/directed targeting) — police extortion, arrests for presentation. This is Severe/High Risk: 0.15-0.25. Given organised-ish targeting, enforcement documented, plus no recourse: score low. Not near-certain execution, but arrest, custody, abuse. I'd say ~0.18.

Dossier 3: Argentina. Strong legal protections, progressive gender identity law, X markers including for non-citizen permanent residents, marriage equality, hate crime law (though aggravator not applied). But current deterioration: 227 hate crimes in 2025 (aggregated, record year), anti-discrimination agency abolished 2024, no national anti-discrimination law covering GI, decrees against care for minors (struck down by court), prison housing decree, trans activists say chaotic. Violence: hate crime count aggregated, no denominator — per rule 16, raw count without denominators carries no magnitude. But "record year" + activists' testimony + prison housing decree = state threat-framing element (tier 1: custody placement by birth sex?). The decree on housing of trans people in prisons — that's resident-focused but prison exposure matters for a traveler if arrested. Hmm, a traveller is unlikely to be imprisoned. But it's a state-level signal.

Overall Argentina has strong institutional protections, X markers, high acceptance polling (LGBT, not trans-specific), but deteriorating climate, violence record. Score maybe 0.70-0.75. Given documented deterioration and hate crime record, maybe 0.68-0.72. I'd say 0.70.

Dossier 4: Croatia-ish (anti-discrimination law 2010, hate crime 2013, but no same-sex marriage, social conservatism — 9.3% would accept LGBT family doctor, 56% say shouldn't show preferences in public, 55% youth wouldn't want homosexual neighbours). No criminalisation. Documented trans bias-violence log: 10 cases in a year, no denominator. Uneven enforcement. No trans-specific targeting by police documented. Social hostility significant: 2022 survey 9.3% accept LGBT doctor — that's high hostility (tier 3) with anti-discrimination recourse that is slow/uneven. Also anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation, not clearly gender identity (the Employment Equal Treatment Act... no that's dossier 5). Dossier 4: 2010 law covers sexual orientation; hate crime covers SO and GI. Constitutional Article 18 removal of SO and GI in 2016 — symbolic but signals hostility. LGR unknown/unresolved.

Score: no criminalisation, no police targeting documented, but pervasive social hostility and weak enforcement. Tier 3. Likely Elevated Risk: ~0.55-0.62. The anti-discrimination law covers SO in employment/services/health; whether GI covered is unclear — hate crime does cover GI. Working recourse somewhat. I'd say 0.58.

Dossier 5: Latvia-ish. Same-sex legal since 1869, no LGR statutory (litigation route), anti-discrimination covers SO explicitly, hate crime on SO, employment protection extended to gender identity 2022. Constitutional "any other status" read as covering SOGI. Daily discrimination, violence, stigmatisation per advocacy. No subnational variation. No trans-specific violence figures. Marriage ban; Feb 2025 court ruling. Overall: no criminalisation, some working protections (employment GI), but no LGR route for visitor anyway, thin social acceptance, some backlash. Score around 0.62-0.68.

Dossier 1: no GI anti-discrimination (workplace law excludes GI), broadcast code hostility, toilet backlash, but strong economy, Pride 28k, 80% youth willingness, gay bars, official prison data no assaults, no trans-specific violence. Dossier 5: employment GI protection, hate crime SO only, daily discrimination and violence reported by civil society, constitutional implicit. Hmm.

Dossier 5 has documented "daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation" per advocacy submission — that's a prevalence statement but fairly general/undated ("still face daily"). Dossier 1 has documented social friction (toilet backlash) but also documented acceptance indicators (Pride crowds, youth survey 80%/75%/58%, prison data no assaults, thriving scene).

I'd rate 1 slightly above 5? Or similar. Dossier 1's youth survey (2021) is LGBT-wide, not trans-specific — per rule 17, not fully qualifying but a general climate signal. Dossier 5's violence statement is also LGBT-wide and unsourced prevalence.

Dossier 5 has working GI employment protection (a real protection but resident-facing, not traveler). Hate crime law covering SO only, not GI. Dossier 1 has no hate crime law covering either, and no GI protection at all.

Dossier 1 has documented no recorded assaults on trans prisoners (positive institutional datum). Dossier 5 has a court precedent supporting gender marker change and constitutional court criticism — institutional culture positive.

Hmm, both roughly similar. I'll set 1 = 0.62, 5 = 0.64? Or 1 = 0.64, 5 = 0.62. Let me consider the toilet backlash: in dossier 1, an actual public backlash and boycott threat over a gender-neutral toilet — that is social hostility toward trans inclusion, weight-bearing but tier 3 at most, and it's about facilities. In dossier 5, no such incident; rather unresolved marriage and litigation-only LGR. Dossier 5's main negatives are reports of daily discrimination/violence (general) and instability. Dossier 1's negatives include a broadcast code clause grouping homosexuality with paedophilia (state media hostility) plus the toilet backlash plus no GI protections.

I think Dossier 5 slightly safer: no documented anti-trans public backlash incident, working employment GI protection, constitutional implicit protection, courts actively engaged. So 5 = 0.65, 1 = 0.61.

Hmm but dossier 5's "daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation" from the advocacy coalition is a documented prevalence claim about society; dossier 1 lacks that but has the toilet backlash.

Let me settle: 1 = 0.62, 5 = 0.65.

Actually reconsider dossier 1 more carefully: Singapore. Actual real-world risk to outed trans traveler: low-to-moderate; no criminalisation, but police could be dismissive, social disapproval, and Section 294 public decency could theoretically bite a visibly trans person in public? Not documented against trans people. The main documented trans-specific friction: LGR surgery gatekeeping (resident), workplace no protection (resident), broadcast code (media), toilet backlash (social). Yet rule 13: "a jurisdiction whose dossier shows (i) no trans-specific criminal offence, (ii) no documented targeting of trans people, and (iii) documented social acceptance of gender diversity ... sits above jurisdictions with similar formal machinery but no documented acceptance." Singapore lacks documented acceptance of gender diversity — it has documented friction. So it's a step below.

Reduced Risk band 0.60-0.80. I'll give 1 = 0.63.

Dossier 5: similar band, 0.65.

Dossier 3 Argentina: strong protections, X markers (visitor-facing positive? X marker recognition on ID cards for non-citizen residents — for a visitor less so but signals document tolerance). But it's a documented pattern of hate crimes against SO/GI people — a state-adjacent signal? It's a record year with activists saying policy made them more vulnerable. Rate maybe 0.68.

Latvia has no LGR, no marriage, but low violence documentation and some protections. For a traveler, Argentina: X markers accepted, strong legal framework, but recent violence rise and government hostility (Milei). Latvia: no criminalisation, employment GI protection, no documented violence counts, some daily discrimination reports.

I'd put Argentina at 0.70 and Latvia 0.65. Fine.

Dossier 2: 0.17.

Let me finalize scores: 1: 0.63, 2: 0.17, 3: 0.70, 4: 0.56, 5: 0.65.

Check dossier 2 isn't too high: police forcing genital display, arrests for gender expression, publicizing names, no recourse, official hostility. That's state targeting with severity 3-4. Not 0.00 (no death penalty for trans). 0.15-0.20 fine.
